*stagna* (n. acc. pl., "pools, waters") *refusa* (perf. pass. part., "poured back, flooded") *vadis* (abl. pl., "onto the shallows") — Neptune observes the waters flooded back onto the shallows. *graviter* (adv., "deeply, heavily") *commotus* (perf. pass. part., "moved, disturbed") — he is deeply disturbed by the disruption. *alto* (abl. n. sg., "from the deep") connects to the next line, positioning Neptune rising from the depths.

lines.original: prospiciens, summa placidum caput extulit unda.
lines.english: Looking out, he raised his calm head above the surface of the wave.
lines.gloss: **prospiciens** (pres. part., nom. sg. m.) "looking out/surveying"; **summa** (abl. sg. f.) "from the top of"; **placidum** (acc. sg. n.) "calm, peaceful"; **caput** (acc. sg. n.) "head"; **extulit** (perf., 3rd sg.) "raised, lifted up"; **unda** (abl. sg. f.) "wave, water." Neptune, looking out over the sea, raised his calm head from the surface of the water, surveying Aeneas's scattered fleet across the expanse.

lines.original: Disiectam Aeneae, toto videt aequore classem,
lines.english: He sees Aeneas' fleet scattered over the whole sea.
lines.gloss: **Disiectam** (perfect passive participle, accusative feminine singular, from *disicio*) "scattered" modifies *classem*. **Aeneae** (genitive singular) "of Aeneas" depends on *classem*. **toto ... aequore** (ablative of place where) "over the whole sea." **videt** (third-person singular present active indicative) "sees." **classem** (accusative singular) "fleet," direct object of *videt*. Neptune sees Aeneas's fleet scattered over the whole sea.

lines.original: fluctibus oppressos Troas caelique ruina,
lines.english: the Trojans overwhelmed by waves and the ruin of heaven
lines.gloss:
**fluctibus oppressos Troas caelique ruina,**

*fluctibus* (m. abl. pl. of *fluctus*) "by the waves"; *oppressos* (perf. pass. part. acc. m. pl. of *opprimo*) "overwhelmed, crushed"; *Troas* (acc. m. pl. of *Troas*) "the Trojans"; *caeli* (gen. sg. of *caelum*) "of the sky"; *ruina* (abl. sg. of *ruina*) "by the ruin, collapse." The Trojans are overwhelmed by the waves and by the collapse/destruction from the sky (Jupiter's storm).

lines.original: nec latuere doli fratrem Iunonis et irae.
lines.english: Nor did the tricks and anger of Juno's brother escape his notice.
lines.gloss:
**nec latuere doli fratrem Iunonis et irae.**

*latuere* (perfect, "escaped the notice of") governs *fratrem* (accusative, "brother," i.e., Neptune); *doli* and *irae* (nominative plural subjects, "the tricks and anger") refer to Juno's scheming; *fratrem Iunonis* identifies Neptune as Juno's brother. The line means "nor did the tricks and anger of Juno escape her brother's notice."

lines.original: Eurum ad se Zephyrumque vocat, dehinc talia fatur:
lines.english: He calls Eurus and Zephyrus to him, then speaks these words:
lines.gloss: **Eurum** (acc. sg., Greek name) "the East Wind," **Zephyrumque** (acc. sg., Greek name) "and the West Wind" – direct objects of **vocat** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic., "he/she calls"). **Dehinc** (adv.) "thereupon, next," **talia** (acc. pl. neut., "such things") – object of **fatur** (3rd sg. pres. dep. indic., "he/she speaks"). Aeolus summons two principal winds and begins his address to them.

lines.original: Tantane vos generis tenuit fiducia vestri?
lines.english: Has confidence in your birth held you so greatly in its grip?
lines.gloss: **Tantane** (interrog. adv.) "so great" modifies *fiducia*; **generis** (gen. sing., neut.) "of birth/lineage"; **tenuit** (perf. act. indic., 3rd sing., *teneo*) "held/seized"; **fiducia** (nom. sing., fem.) "confidence/presumption"; **vestri** (gen. sing., masc.) "of your own" modifying *generis*. Juno rebukes the winds: "Has so great a confidence in your own birth/station seized you?"

lines.original: Iam caelum terramque meo sine numine, venti,
lines.english: Now do you dare, winds, without my divine will to mix sky and earth
lines.gloss: **caelum** (noun, acc. sg.) "sky, heaven"; **terramque** (noun, acc. sg. with enclitic -que) "and earth"; **numine** (noun, abl. sg.) "divine will, power"; **sine** (preposition + abl.) "without"; **venti** (noun, voc. pl.) "O winds." Neptune rebukes the winds for daring to confound sky and earth without his divine authority, establishing the hierarchical order among the gods.

lines.original: miscere, et tantas audetis tollere moles?
lines.english: To mingle, and do you dare raise up such massive waves?
lines.gloss:
**miscere** (pres. inf., "to mix/stir up"), **et** (conj., "and"), **tantas** (acc. pl. f., "such great"), **audetis** (2nd pl. pres. ind., "you dare"), **tollere** (pres. inf., "to raise/lift up"), **moles** (acc. pl. f., "masses/structures"). 

Neptune rebukes the winds for daring to churn up the sea and sky and raise such enormous waves without his divine authorization, an angry interrogative expressing his outrage at their presumption.

lines.original: Quos ego—sed motos praestat componere fluctus.
lines.english: You whom I—but it is better first to calm the troubled waves.
lines.gloss:
**Quos ego—sed motos praestat componere fluctus.**

*Quos* (relative pronoun, acc. pl. masc.) = "whom" (object of implied verb of punishment). *Ego* (personal pronoun, nom. sing.) = "I" (Neptune breaking off his threat). *Motos* (perfect passive participle, acc. pl. masc., from *moveo*) = "disturbed/stirred up." *Praestat* (verb, 3rd sing. pres. act. indic., from *praesto*) = "it is better/preferable." *Componere* (infinitive, pres. act.) = "to calm/settle." Neptune interrupts his threat (*aposiopesis*) to prioritize calming the storm-tossed waves over punishing the winds.

lines.original: Post mihi non simili poena commissa luetis.
lines.english: Hereafter you shall not atone for misdeeds with a similar punishment.
lines.gloss: **Post** (adv., "hereafter, in the future") **mihi** (dat. of ego, "to me, before me") **non** (neg. particle) **simili** (abl. of similis, modifying poena, "with a similar") **poena** (abl. of poena, "penalty, punishment") **commissa** (neut. pl. acc. of commissum, "offenses, crimes") **luetis** (2nd pl. fut. of luo, "you will pay for, atone for"). Neptune warns the winds that future transgressions will not be punished with mere verbal rebuke but with far severer consequences.

lines.original: Maturate fugam, regique haec dicite vestro:
lines.english: Hasten your flight and say these things to your king:
lines.gloss:
**Maturate fugam, regique haec dicite vestro:**

*Maturate* (2nd pl. pres. imper. act. of *maturo*) = "hasten"; *fugam* (acc. sg. f.) = "flight, escape"; *regi* (dat. sg. m.) = "to the king"; *haec* (acc. pl. n.) = "these things"; *dicite* (2nd pl. pres. imper. act. of *dico*) = "say, tell"; *vestro* (dat. sg. m.) = "your." Neptune commands the winds to hasten their flight and report his words to their king Aeolus, asserting his own supreme authority over the sea.

lines.original: non illi imperium pelagi saevumque tridentem,
lines.english: Not to him was given the empire of the sea and savage trident,
lines.gloss:
**non illi imperium pelagi saevumque tridentem,**

*imperium* (n. nom./acc. sg.) "power, sovereignty"; *pelagi* (n. gen. sg. from *pelagus*) "of the sea"; *saevum* (adj. acc. sg. n.) "savage, cruel"; *tridentem* (m. acc. sg.) "trident." Neptune asserts that Neptune (the speaker), not Jupiter (*illi* dative of possession), holds dominion over the sea and its fearsome trident—establishing territorial divine authority.

lines.original: sed mihi sorte datum. Tenet ille immania saxa,
lines.english: but given to me by lot. He holds those monstrous rocks, your home, Eurus.
lines.gloss: **sorte** (ablative singular of *sors*) "by lot, by allotment"; **datum** (perfect passive participle of *do*, accusative neuter singular agreeing with *imperium*) "given"; **tenet** (3rd singular present active of *teneo*) "he holds, possesses"; **immania** (accusative neuter plural of *immanis*) "monstrous, huge"; **saxa** (accusative neuter plural of *saxum*) "rocks, crags." Neptune contrasts his divinely allotted sea-dominion with Aeolus's assigned realm of massive rocky caves.

lines.original: vestras, Eure, domos; illa se iactet in aula
lines.english: your homes, Eurus; let him boast himself in that hall
lines.gloss:
**vestras, Eure, domos; illa se iactet in aula**

*vestras* (adj., acc. pl. fem.) "your" modifies *domos*; *Eure* (voc. sg. m.) "Eurus" (the East Wind), vocative address; *domos* (acc. pl. fem.) "homes, halls"; *illa* (abl. sg. fem.) "in that" refers to the domain just mentioned; *iactet* (pres. subj. 3rd sg.) "let him boast, swagger." Juno tells Aeolus to confine himself to the winds' realm, letting Aeolus strut about in that hall rather than anywhere else.

lines.original: Aeolus, et clauso ventorum carcere regnet.
lines.english: Aeolus, and let him rule in the closed prison of the winds.
lines.gloss: **Aeolus** (nom. sg., proper noun) "Aeolus"; **clauso** (abl. sg. m., perfect passive participle of *claudo*) "closed, shut up"; **ventorum** (gen. pl. m., *ventus*) "of the winds"; **carcere** (abl. sg. m., *carcer*) "in the prison"; **regnet** (3rd sg. pres. subj., *regno*) "let him rule/reign." Venus tells Aeolus to rule from his palace while keeping the winds shut in their prison.

lines.original: Sic ait, et dicto citius tumida aequora placat,
lines.english: So he speaks, and swifter than the word he calms the swelling seas.
lines.gloss:
**Gloss:**

*Sic* (adv., "thus") introduces Neptune's swift action. *ait* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *aio*, "he speaks"). *dicto* (abl. sg. neut. of *dictum*, "than the word/speech," with comparative *citius*). *citius* (comp. adv., "more swiftly"). *tumida* (nom./acc. pl. neut. of *tumidus*, "swollen") modifies *aequora*. *aequora* (acc. pl. neut. of *aequor*, "seas/waters," dir. obj. of *placat*). *placat* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *placo*, "he calms").

lines.original: collectasque fugat nubes, solemque reducit.
lines.english: He scatters the gathered clouds and brings back the sun.
lines.gloss:
**collectasque fugat nubes, solemque reducit.**

*collectas* (perf. pass. part. acc. fem. pl. from *colligo*) "gathered," modifying *nubes*; *fugat* (pres. act. ind. 3rd sg. from *fugo*) "puts to flight, disperses"; *nubes* (acc. fem. pl.) "clouds"; *solemque* (*solem* + *-que*) "and the sun" (acc. masc. sg.); *reducit* (pres. act. ind. 3rd sg. from *reduco*) "leads back, restores." Neptune disperses the storm clouds he has gathered and brings back the sunlight.

lines.original: Cymothoe simul et Triton adnixus acuto
lines.english: Cymothoe and Triton, straining against the sharp rock together, thrust the ships free.
lines.gloss:
**Cymothoe simul et Triton adnixus acuto**

*Cymothoe* (nom. sg., Greek name): sea-nymph Cymothoe, subject with Triton; *simul* (adv.): at the same time, together; *Triton* (nom. sg.): sea-god Triton, joint subject; *adnixus* (perf. part. nom. sg. m.): having pressed against, straining with; *acuto* (abl. sg. n.): with his sharp (trident, understood from context). The sea-nymph Cymothoe and the god Triton work together, Triton straining with his sharp trident to free Neptune's ships from the rocks.

lines.original: detrudunt navis scopulo; levat ipse tridenti;
lines.english: They thrust the ships from the sharp rock; he himself lifts them with his trident.
lines.gloss:
**detrudunt navis scopulo; levat ipse tridenti;**

*detrudunt* (3rd pl. pres. act. ind. of *detrudo*) "they thrust down/dislodge"; *navis* (acc. pl. f.) "the ships"; *scopulo* (abl. sing. m.) "from the rock/reef"; *levat* (3rd sing. pres. act. ind. of *levo*) "he lifts/raises"; *tridenti* (abl. sing. m.) "with his trident." Neptune personally assists Cymothoe and Triton by lifting ships with his trident, dislodging them from the rocks where they are grounded.

lines.original: et vastas aperit syrtis, et temperat aequor,
lines.english: and he opens the vast shoals and calms the sea
lines.gloss:
**et vastas aperit syrtis, et temperat aequor,**

*aperit* (3rd sg. pres. ind. act., *aperio*) "opens up"; *syrtis* (acc. pl., *syrtis* f.) "sandbanks, shoals"; *vastas* (acc. pl. f., *vastus*) "vast, extensive"; *temperat* (3rd sg. pres. ind. act., *tempero*) "calms, controls"; *aequor* (acc. sg. n., *aequor*) "sea, level surface." Neptune opens up the vast sandbanks (making passage possible) and calms the sea with his trident.

lines.original: atque rotis summas levibus perlabitur undas.
lines.english: and glides over the topmost waves with his light wheels.
lines.gloss:
**atque** (conj.) "and"; **rotis** (abl. pl. of *rota*, f.) "with wheels/chariots"; **summas** (acc. pl. f. of *summus*) "topmost, surface"; **levibus** (abl. pl. of *levis*) "light, swift"; **perlabitur** (3rd sg. pres. ind. of *perlabor*, deponent) "glides over." 

Neptune glides over the topmost waves with his swift chariot wheels, calming the storm-tossed sea after opening the sandbanks and tempering the waters.

lines.original: Ac veluti magno in populo cum saepe coorta est
lines.english: And just as when often in a great people sedition has arisen
lines.gloss:
**Ac veluti magno in populo cum saepe coorta est**

*veluti* (adv.) "just as"; *magno in populo* (abl. of place) "in a great populace/nation"; *cum* (conj.) "when"; *saepe* (adv.) "often"; *coorta est* (perf. indic., 3rd sg. of *coorior*) "has arisen." This simile introduces a comparison between Neptune calming the waves and a statesman quelling civil unrest, with *seditio* as the understood subject carried over from the next line.

lines.original: seditio, saevitque animis ignobile volgus,
lines.english: and sedition rages, and the base-born mob grows savage in spirit
lines.gloss:
**seditio, saevitque animis ignobile volgus,**

*seditio* (nom. sg. f.): "sedition, civil strife" (subject of understood verb); *saevit* (pres. ind. 3rd sg.): "rages, acts savagely" (*-que* = "and"); *animis* (abl. pl. m.): "in their spirits/passions" (ablative of respect or means); *ignobile* (nom. sg. n.): "lowborn, base"; *volgus* (nom. sg. n.): "the mob, common crowd" (subject). The sedition erupts and the base mob rages in its passions, continuing the extended simile of civil unrest.

lines.original: iamque faces et saxa volant—furor arma ministrat;
lines.english: Now torches and stones fly—fury supplies the weapons.
lines.gloss:
**iamque faces et saxa volant—furor arma ministrat;**

*iamque* (adv., "and now/already"); *faces* (nom. pl., "torches"); *saxa* (nom. pl., "stones"); *volant* (3rd pl. pres., "fly/are flying"); *furor* (nom. sg., "madness/rage"); *arma* (acc. pl., "weapons"); *ministrat* (3rd sg. pres., "supplies/furnishes"). The violence escalates as projectiles fly through the air, with madness itself personified as the supplier of weapons to the rioting mob.

lines.original: tum, pietate gravem ac meritis si forte virum quem
lines.english: Then, if by chance they catch sight of some man weighty in devotion and merit
lines.gloss: **tum** (adv.) "then"; **pietate** (abl. of *pietas*) "in devotion/duty"; **gravem** (acc. masc. sing. of *gravis*) "weighty, respected," modifying *virum*; **meritis** (abl. pl. of *meritum*) "in achievements/services"; **virum** (acc. masc. sing. of *vir*) "man." The line introduces a conditional protasis: "then, if by chance they catch sight of some man respected for his devotion and achievements."

lines.original: conspexere, silent, arrectisque auribus adstant;
lines.english: If they catch sight of a man weighty in duty and merit, they fall silent and stand with ears alert.
lines.gloss: **conspexere** (perf. indic. 3rd pl., *conspicio*) "they catch sight of [him]"; **silent** (pres. indic. 3rd pl., *sileo*) "they fall silent"; **arrectis ... auribus** (abl. pl., *arrigo + auris*) "with ears pricked up"; **adstant** (pres. indic. 3rd pl., *adsto*) "they stand by/attend." The rioters, upon seeing a man grave with piety and merit, immediately quiet down and stand attentively with ears raised to listen.

lines.original: ille regit dictis animos, et pectora mulcet,—
lines.english: He governs their spirits with words and soothes their hearts—
lines.gloss: **ille** (nom. sg. m. demonstrative pronoun) "that one" (i.e., Neptune); **regit** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *rego*) "rules, guides"; **dictis** (abl. pl. n. of *dictum*) "with words"; **animos** (acc. pl. m. of *animus*) "spirits, passions"; **mulcet** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *mulceo*) "soothes, calms." Neptune governs the passions of the winds with his words and soothes their hearts, restoring calm to the turbulent sea.

lines.original: sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor, aequora postquam
lines.english: Thus all the roar of the sea fell silent, after the father looked forth and rode through the open sky.
lines.gloss:
**Target: sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor, aequora postquam**

*sic* (adv.): "thus, in this way"; *cunctus* (nom. sg. m.): "all, entire"; *pelagi* (gen. sg.): "of the sea"; *cecidit* (perf. 3rd sg.): "fell, subsided"; *fragor* (nom. sg. m.): "crash, roar, din"; *aequora* (acc. pl. n.): "seas, waters, surface"; *postquam* (conj.): "after." Thus fell all the roar of the sea, after the father (Neptune) looking forth and borne through the open sky (calmed it with his words).

lines.original: prospiciens genitor caeloque invectus aperto
lines.english: The father looking forth and borne through the open sky
lines.gloss: **prospiciens** (pres. part., nom. sing. masc.) "looking out over" — **genitor** (nom. sing.) "father" [Neptune] — **caeloque** (dat. sing., -que "and") "and to/in the sky" — **invectus** (perf. part., nom. sing. masc.) "having been borne, riding" — **aperto** (abl. sing. neut.) "open, clear." The father Neptune, looking out over the sea, rides through the now-clear sky, having calmed the storm.

lines.original: flectit equos, curruque volans dat lora secundo.
lines.english: He turns his horses and flying on his favoring chariot gives them free rein.
lines.gloss:
**flectit equos, curruque volans dat lora secundo.**

*flectit* (3rd sg. pres. act. ind. of *flecto*) "turns, steers"; *equos* (acc. pl. m. of *equus*) "horses"; *curru* (abl. sg. m. of *currus*) "chariot"; *volans* (pres. act. ptcp. nom. sg. of *volo*) "flying"; *lora* (acc. pl. n. of *lorum*) "reins"; *secundo* (abl. sg. m./n. of *secundus*) "following, favorable." Jupiter turns his horses and, flying in his chariot, gives the reins free rein to his favorable course.

lines.original: Defessi Aeneadae, quae proxima litora, cursu
lines.english: The weary followers of Aeneas make for the nearest shores in their course
lines.gloss: **Defessi** (perf. pass. part., nom. pl. masc., from *defetiscor*) "exhausted"; **Aeneadae** (nom. pl., "sons/companions of Aeneas"); **proxima** (superl. adj., nom./acc. pl. neut., "nearest"); **litora** (acc. pl. neut., "shores"); **cursu** (abl. sg. masc., "in their course/by sailing"). The weary Trojans head toward whatever shores are nearest in their course, transitioning from Juno's storm to their landing in Libya.

lines.original: contendunt petere, et Libyae vertuntur ad oras.
lines.english: They strive to reach the nearest shores and turn toward the coasts of Libya.
lines.gloss: **contendunt** (3rd pl. pres. ind. act., *contendō*) "they strive"; **petere** (pres. act. inf., *petō*) "to seek"; **vertuntur** (3rd pl. pres. ind. pass., *vertō*) "they turn"; **ad oras** (acc. pl. f., *ōra*) "toward the shores." The weary Trojans strain to reach the nearest coastline and turn toward the shores of Libya.

lines.original: Est in secessu longo locus: insula portum
lines.english: There is a place in a long recess: an island forms a harbor
lines.gloss:
**Est in secessu longo locus: insula portum**

*est* (3rd sg. pres. ind. of *sum*) "there is"; *secessu* (abl. sg. m. of *secessus*) "in a recess/withdrawal"; *longo* (abl. sg. m. of *longus*) "deep/far-extending"; *locus* (nom. sg. m.) "a place"; *insula* (nom. sg. f.) "an island"; *portum* (acc. sg. m. of *portus*) "harbor" (object of *efficit* in the following line). This introduces the harbor at Libya where Aeneas's fleet will find refuge; the island forms a harbor through the projection of its sides.

lines.original: efficit obiectu laterum, quibus omnis ab alto
lines.english: An island forms a harbor by the barrier of its sides, against which every wave from the deep is broken and divides itself into receding inlets.
lines.gloss:
**efficit obiectu laterum, quibus omnis ab alto**

*efficit* (3rd sg. pres. act. ind. of *efficiō*) "makes" or "forms" — the island creates the harbor; *obiectū* (abl. sg. masc. of *obiectus*, -ūs) "by the blocking" or "by the projection" — ablative of means; *laterum* (gen. pl. neut. of *latus*, lateris) "of the sides" — the island's flanking promontories; *quibus* (abl. pl. neut. of *quī*, relative pronoun) "by which" or "off which"; *ab altō* (abl. sg. neut. of *altum*) "from the deep sea." The island's projecting sides create the harbor by breaking waves coming from the open ocean.

lines.original: frangitur inque sinus scindit sese unda reductos.
lines.english: The wave breaks and divides itself into receding inlets.
lines.gloss:
**frangitur** (3rd sg. pres. pass. indic. of *frango*) "is broken"; **sinus** (acc. pl. m. of *sinus*) "bays, curves"; **scindit** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *scindo*) "splits, divides"; **sese** (acc. of reflexive *se*) "itself"; **reductos** (acc. pl. m. perf. pass. part. of *reduco*) "drawn back, receding."

The wave breaks upon the barrier of rocks and divides itself into the receding bays formed by the lateral projections, describing how the harbor's architecture channels incoming water into protected inlets.

lines.original: Hinc atque hinc vastae rupes geminique minantur
lines.english: On this side and that vast cliffs and twin crags threaten toward the sky.
lines.gloss:
**Hinc atque hinc vastae rupes geminique minantur**

*hinc atque hinc* (adv.) "on this side and on that," "on both sides"; *vastae* (adj., nom. pl. f.) "vast," "huge," modifying *rupes*; *rupes* (noun, nom. pl. f.) "cliffs," "rocks," subject; *gemini* (adj., nom. pl. m.) "twin," "twofold," substantive used as subject; *minantur* (verb, 3rd pl. pres. indic. deponent) "threaten," "loom menacingly." The twin cliffs rise threateningly on both sides of the harbor entrance.

lines.original: in caelum scopuli, quorum sub vertice late
lines.english: skyward rocks, beneath whose peak far and wide
lines.gloss:
**in caelum scopuli, quorum sub vertice late**

*scopuli* (nom. pl., "cliffs/crags") serve as subject; *in caelum* (acc., "into the sky") indicates their soaring height; *quorum* (gen. pl. relative pronoun, "of which") introduces a subordinate clause; *sub vertice* (abl. sg., "beneath the peak/summit") gives location; *late* (adverb, "widely") modifies what lies spread beneath. The cliffs tower skyward, and beneath their peak something extends broadly—likely the calm waters mentioned in the following line.

lines.original: aequora tuta silent; tum silvis scaena coruscis
lines.english: The safe waters lie silent; then above a stage of shimmering woods and a grove looms dark with bristling shade.
lines.gloss:
**aequora tuta silent; tum silvis scaena coruscis**

*aequora* (nom. pl. n., "waters/sea-surfaces") *tuta* (nom. pl. n., "safe/protected") *silent* (3rd pl. pres., "are silent/still"); *tum* (adv., "then/moreover"); *silvis* (abl. pl. f., "with woods/forests") *scaena* (nom. sg. f., "stage/backdrop/scene") *coruscis* (abl. pl. f., "shimmering/waving"). The protected waters lie calm and silent; then/above, a theatrical backdrop gleams with quivering forests.

lines.original: desuper horrentique atrum nemus imminet umbra.
lines.english: Above a dark grove looms over with its bristling shade.
lines.gloss: **desuper** (adverb): "from above"; **horrenti** (present participle, ablative singular): "bristling, shaggy"; **atrum** (adjective, nominative/accusative singular neuter): "dark, black"; **nemus** (noun, nominative singular neuter): "grove, wood"; **imminet** (verb, 3rd person singular present): "overhangs, looms over"; **umbra** (noun, ablative singular): "with shade/shadow." A dark grove looms from above with bristling/shaggy shadow, continuing the description of the foreboding grotto setting.

lines.original: Fronte sub adversa scopulis pendentibus antrum,
lines.english: Beneath the opposing cliff is a cave with overhanging rocks.
lines.gloss:
**Fronte sub adversa scopulis pendentibus antrum,**

*Fronte* (abl. sg. f., "frons"): "beneath the brow/face," indicating position. *adversa* (abl. sg. f., "adversus"): "opposite, facing." *scopulis pendentibus* (abl. pl. m./n., "scopulus" + pres. part. "pendeo"): "with hanging/overhanging rocks." *antrum* (nom. sg. n.): "cave, grotto," the subject. The line describes a cave beneath an opposing cliff-face with rocks hanging overhead, continuing the description of the nymphs' sacred grove.

lines.original: intus aquae dulces vivoque sedilia saxo,
lines.english: Within are fresh waters and seats of living rock, a home of nymphs.
lines.gloss:
**intus aquae dulces vivoque sedilia saxo**

*intus* (adv.): "within, inside"; *aquae dulces* (nom. pl., f.): "fresh/sweet waters"; *vivo saxo* (abl. sg., n.): "from living/natural rock," ablative of material; *sedilia* (nom. pl., n.): "seats, benches." Inside the cave are fresh waters and seats formed from living rock, completing the description of the nymphs' grotto as a natural harbor requiring no artificial moorings.

lines.original: nympharum domus: hic fessas non vincula navis
lines.english: the home of nymphs: here no cables hold the weary ships
lines.gloss:
**nympharum domus: hic fessas non vincula navis**

*nympharum* (gen. pl. fem., "of the nymphs") modifies *domus* (nom. sg. fem., "home, dwelling"); *hic* (adv., "here"); *fessas* (acc. pl. fem., "weary, tired") modifies *navis* (acc. pl. fem., "ships"); *vincula* (nom. pl. neut., "chains, cables") serves as subject with *non* ("not") negating the understood verb. This describes the harbor as a home of nymphs where weary ships need no restraining cables.

lines.original: ulla tenent, unco non alligat ancora morsu.
lines.english: No cables hold the weary ships here, nor does the anchor bind them fast with hooked bite.
lines.gloss: **ulla** (nom. sg. neut., "any"), **tenent** (3rd pl. pres. act. indic. of *teneo*, "hold/restrain"), **unco** (abl. sg. masc./neut. of *uncus -a -um*, "hooked/curved"), **ancora** (nom. sg. fem., "anchor"), **morsu** (abl. sg. masc. of *morsus*, "bite/grip"). No chains hold the weary ships, nor does an anchor secure them with its hooked bite—the natural harbor requires no mooring equipment.

lines.original: Huc septem Aeneas collectis navibus omni
lines.english: Here Aeneas with seven ships gathered from all their number comes in.
lines.gloss: **Huc** (adverb) = "hither, to this place"; **septem** (indeclinable numeral adjective) = "seven," modifying *navibus*; **Aeneas** (nominative singular, proper noun) = "Aeneas," subject; **collectis** (perfect passive participle, ablative plural, modifying *navibus*) = "having been gathered/collected"; **navibus** (ablative plural, *navis*, -is f.) = "with ships," ablative of accompaniment; **omni** (ablative singular, *omnis*, -e*) = "from all," modifying an understood noun or used absolutely. Aeneas arrives at this place with seven ships gathered from the entire fleet.

lines.original: ex numero subit; ac magno telluris amore
lines.english: and from all their number he approaches land, and with great love of solid ground
lines.gloss:
**ex numero subit; ac magno telluris amore**

*ex numero* – "from the (full) number/fleet"; ablative of separation. *subit* – 3rd sg. pres. indic. of *subeo*, "he approaches, comes to shore." *magno...amore* – ablative of manner, "with great love/desire." *telluris* – gen. sg. of *tellus*, "of the land/earth," objective genitive with *amore*. Aeneas arrives with seven ships salvaged from the total fleet, and his men disembark with great longing for solid ground.

lines.original: egressi optata potiuntur Troes harena,
lines.english: Landing, the Trojans take possession of the longed-for sand.
lines.gloss:
**egressi**: perfect participle of *egredior*, nominative plural masculine, "having disembarked" or "having gone out"
**optata**: perfect passive participle of *opto*, ablative singular feminine (modifying *harena*), "longed-for" or "desired"
**potiuntur**: present indicative, 3rd person plural deponent of *potior* (+ ablative), "take possession of" or "gain control of"
**Troes**: nominative plural, "the Trojans"
**harena**: ablative singular feminine, "sand" or "shore"

The Trojans, having disembarked, take possession of the longed-for shore, finally reaching land after their海上ordeal.

lines.original: et sale tabentis artus in litore ponunt.
lines.english: and lay their sea-drenched limbs upon the shore.
lines.gloss:
**et sale tabentis artus in litore ponunt.**

*sale* (ablative of *sal*, m.) "with/in salt(water)"; *tabentis* (present participle accusative plural of *tabesco*) "wasting away, dripping, drenched"; *artus* (accusative plural of *artus*, m.) "limbs, bodies"; *litore* (ablative of *litus*, n.) "on the shore"; *ponunt* (3rd plural present active of *pono*) "they place, set down." The Trojans lay down their salt-soaked, exhausted limbs on the shore after landing.

lines.original: Ac primum silici scintillam excudit Achates,
lines.english: And first Achates struck a spark from flint
lines.gloss:
**Ac primum silici scintillam excudit Achates,**

*primum* (adv.) "first"; *silici* (noun, abl. sing. of *silex*) "from flint"; *scintillam* (noun, acc. sing.) "a spark"; *excudit* (verb, 3rd sing. perf. act.) "struck out"; *Achates* (proper noun, nom. sing.) "Achates" (Aeneas's faithful companion). Achates first strikes a spark from flint, initiating the fire-making process to dry and warm the storm-tossed survivors.

lines.original: succepitque ignem foliis, atque arida circum
lines.english: He caught the fire in leaves and placed dry kindling around and quickly seized the flame in tinder.
lines.gloss:
**succepitque ignem foliis, atque arida circum**

*succepitque* (succipio, perfect, "and he caught/received"); *ignem* (ignis, acc. sg., "fire"); *foliis* (folium, abl. pl., "with leaves"); *arida* (aridus, neut. acc. pl., "dry things/tinder"); *circum* (adv., "around"). Achates catches the spark in leaves and places dry kindling around it to nurture the nascent flame.

lines.original: nutrimenta dedit, rapuitque in fomite flammam.
lines.english: He gave it fuel all around and quickly caught the flame in the tinder.
lines.gloss: **nutrimenta** (n. acc. pl., from *nutrimentum*) = "fuel, nourishment"; **dedit** (perf. 3rd sg., *do*) = "gave, provided"; **rapuit** (perf. 3rd sg., *rapio*) = "seized, snatched up"; **fomite** (m. abl. sg., *fomes*) = "tinder, kindling"; **flammam** (f. acc. sg., *flamma*) = "flame." He provided dry fuel (to the leaves mentioned in the previous line) and quickly caught/kindled a flame in the tinder.

lines.original: Tum Cererem corruptam undis Cerealiaque arma
lines.english: Then weary of their trials they ready Ceres corrupted by the waves and Ceres' tools.
lines.gloss: **Tum** (adv.) "then"; **Cererem** (acc. sing., f.) "Ceres/grain," goddess of grain or metonymy for wheat; **corruptam** (perf. pass. part., acc. sing., f.) "spoiled, corrupted"; **undis** (abl. pl., f.) "by the waves/water"; **Cerealia** (adj., acc. pl., n.) "of Ceres, grain-related"; **arma** (acc. pl., n.) "tools, implements" (here, mills and ovens for processing grain). The Trojans prepare their wave-damaged grain and the implements of Ceres for making bread.

lines.original: expediunt fessi rerum, frugesque receptas
lines.english: Weary from their trials, they make ready the recovered grain and Ceres' tools.
lines.gloss: **expediunt** (verb, 3rd pl. pres. indic. of *expedio*) "they prepare, set out"; **fessi** (adj., nom. pl. masc., perf. pass. part. of *fatiscor/fateor*) "weary, exhausted"; **rerum** (noun, gen. pl. of *res*) "of affairs, circumstances"; **fruges** (noun, acc. pl. of *frux*) "grain, crops"; **receptas** (adj., acc. pl. fem., perf. pass. part. of *recipio*) "recovered, rescued." The weary sailors prepare the grain they have salvaged from the sea, readying it for drying and grinding despite its water-damaged state.

lines.original: et torrere parant flammis et frangere saxo.
lines.english: They prepare to roast them over flames and crush the grain with stone.
lines.gloss:
**et torrere parant flammis et frangere saxo.**

*torrere* (pres. act. inf., "to parch/roast") and *frangere* (pres. act. inf., "to break/crush") are complementary infinitives with *parant* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic., "they prepare"). *flammis* (abl. pl., "with flames") and *saxo* (abl. sg., "with stone/millstone") are ablatives of means. The Trojans prepare to roast and grind their recovered grain after their shipwreck.

lines.original: Aeneas scopulum interea conscendit, et omnem
lines.english: Meanwhile Aeneas climbed a cliff, and sought the whole
lines.gloss:
**Aeneas scopulum interea conscendit, et omnem**

*Aeneas* (nom. sg.): "Aeneas," subject. *scopulum* (acc. sg. m., *scopulus*): "cliff, crag," direct object. *interea* (adv.): "meanwhile." *conscendit* (3rd sg. pres./perf. indic., *conscendo*): "climbs, ascends." *omnem* (acc. sg. m./f., *omnis*): "all, the whole," modifying *prospectum* in the following line.

lines.original: prospectum late pelago petit, Anthea si quem
lines.english: He seeks a wide view over the sea, to see if he might spot Antheus anywhere tossed by the wind and the Phrygian galleys.
lines.gloss:
**Gloss on Target Line:**

*prospectum* (acc. sg. m., perfect passive participle of *prospicio*) "view, prospect"; *late* (adv.) "widely, far and wide"; *pelago* (abl. sg. n., *pelagus*) "over/on the sea"; *petit* (3rd sg. pres. indic. act., *peto*) "seeks, searches for"; *si quem* (conditional conj. + acc. sg. m., *quis/qui*) "if any(one)," introducing an indirect question depending on *videat*. Aeneas seeks a wide view over the sea to see if he might spot anyone—specifically Antheus or the other storm-tossed companions.

lines.original: iactatum vento videat Phrygiasque biremis,
lines.english: to see if he might spot Antheus tossed by the wind and the Phrygian galleys
lines.gloss:
**iactatum vento videat Phrygiasque biremis,**

*iactatum* (perf. pass. part. of iacio, acc. masc. sing.) "tossed, driven"; *vento* (abl. masc. sing.) "by the wind"; *videat* (pres. subj. 3rd sing. of video) "he might see"; *Phrygiasque* (adj. acc. fem. pl., -que = "and") "and Phrygian/Trojan"; *biremis* (acc. fem. pl.) "two-oared ships, biremes." Aeneas scans the sea hoping to spot Antheus or any other storm-tossed companion with their Trojan vessels.

lines.original: aut Capyn, aut celsis in puppibus arma Caici.
lines.english: or Capys, or the arms of Caicus on the lofty sterns.
lines.gloss:
**aut Capyn, aut celsis in puppibus arma Caici.**

*aut...aut* (conjunction): "either...or"; *Capyn* (acc. sing., Greek name): Capys, one of Aeneas's companions; *celsis* (abl. pl., adj.): "lofty, high," modifying *puppibus*; *puppibus* (abl. pl.): "sterns, poops" of ships; *arma* (acc. pl., noun): "arms, weapons"; *Caici* (gen. sing., Greek name): "of Caicus," another Trojan companion. Aeneas surveys the sea hoping to spot either Capys or the weapons/insignia of Caicus on the high sterns of ships, but sees none of his scattered fleet.

lines.original: Navem in conspectu nullam, tris litore cervos
lines.english: He sees no ship in sight, but three stags on the shore wandering.
lines.gloss:
**Navem in conspectu nullam, tris litore cervos**

*Navem* (acc. sg. f., "ship") is the direct object negated by *nullam* (acc. sg. f., "no/not any"). *Conspectu* (abl. sg. m., "sight/view") follows the prepositional phrase *in conspectu* ("in sight"). *Tris* (acc. pl. m., "three," archaic/poetic form of *tres*) modifies *cervos* (acc. pl. m., "stags/deer"), while *litore* (abl. sg. m./n., "shore") indicates location. The verse contrasts the absence of ships with the presence of deer on the shore.

lines.original: prospicit errantis; hos tota armenta sequuntur
lines.english: He spies three stags wandering on the shore; whole herds follow these from behind.
lines.gloss: **prospicit** (verb, 3rd sg. pres. act. indic., *prospicere*) "he catches sight of" — **errantis** (verb, pres. act. part. acc. masc. pl., *errare*) "wandering" — **hos** (pronoun, acc. masc. pl.) "these" — **armenta** (noun, nom. neut. pl.) "herds" — **sequuntur** (verb, 3rd pl. pres. act. indic., *sequi*) "follow." Aeneas spies wandering stags; the entire herds follow behind these leaders.

lines.original: a tergo, et longum per vallis pascitur agmen.
lines.english: from behind, and a long column grazes through the valleys.
lines.gloss: **a tergo** (adverbial phrase: "from behind"); **longum agmen** (acc. neut. adj. + acc. neut. noun: "long column/train"); **vallis** (acc. fem. pl. or gen. fem. sg.: "valleys"); **pascitur** (3rd sg. pres. indic. pass. of *pascor*: "grazes/feeds"). The long train of animals grazes through the valleys from behind, extending the visual sequence of the wandering herd.

lines.original: Constitit hic, arcumque manu celerisque sagittas
lines.english: Here he halted and seized in his hand the bow and swift arrows.
lines.gloss: **Constitit** (perfect, 3rd singular of *consistere*) "he halted/took his stand"; **hic** (adverb) "here"; **arcumque** (*arcus*, accusative singular masculine) "and the bow"; **celerisque** (*celer*, accusative plural feminine) "and swift"; **sagittas** (*sagitta*, accusative plural feminine) "arrows." Aeneas stops and takes up the bow and swift arrows that his faithful companion Achates was carrying.

lines.original: corripuit, fidus quae tela gerebat Achates;
lines.english: He seized the bow and swift arrows, weapons which faithful Achates carried.
lines.gloss:
**corripuit, fidus quae tela gerebat Achates;**

*corripuit* (3rd sg. perf. act. ind., *corripio*) "he snatched up"; *fidus* (nom. sg. m., adj.) "faithful"; *tela* (acc. pl. n., *telum*) "weapons/missiles"; *gerebat* (3rd sg. imperf. act. ind., *gero*) "was carrying"; *Achates* (nom. sg. m.) "Achates" (Aeneas's loyal companion). Aeneas seizes the bow and swift arrows that faithful Achates was bearing, preparing to hunt the deer whose leaders he will target first.

lines.original: ductoresque ipsos primum, capita alta ferentis
lines.english: and first the leaders themselves, bearing their heads high with branching antlers, he lays low
lines.gloss:
**ductoresque ipsos primum, capita alta ferentis**

*ductoresque* (acc. pl. m., "and the leaders") – compound object with *ipsos* emphasizing the leaders themselves; *primum* (adv., "first") marks temporal priority in Aeneas's hunting; *capita alta* (acc. pl. n., "high heads," i.e., with lofty antlers) is the direct object of *ferentis* (acc. pl. m., pres. part. of *fero*, "bearing/carrying"), which modifies *ductoresque*. Aeneas first strikes down the stag-leaders themselves, distinguished by their towering antlers.

lines.original: cornibus arboreis, sternit, tum volgus, et omnem
lines.english: with tree-like antlers he lays low, then the herd, and all the throng
lines.gloss:
**cornibus arboreis, sternit, tum volgus, et omnem**

*cornibus* (neuter ablative plural of *cornu*): "with horns," ablative of means. *arboreis* (ablative plural of *arboreus, -a, -um*): "tree-like, branching," modifying *cornibus*. *sternit* (3rd singular present active indicative of *sterno, -ere*): "he lays low, strikes down," describing the killing of stags. *volgus* (neuter accusative singular): "the common herd, the mass." Aeneas first kills the leaders with branching antlers, then massacres the entire herd of deer.

lines.original: miscet agens telis nemora inter frondea turbam;
lines.english: He scatters them driving the whole throng with weapons through the leafy groves in confusion.
lines.gloss:
**miscet** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *misceō*) "throws into confusion"; **agens** (pres. act. participle of *agō*) "driving"; **telis** (abl. pl. of *tēlum*) "with weapons"; **nemora** (acc. pl. neut. of *nemus*) "groves/woodlands"; **turbam** (acc. sg. fem. of *turba*) "crowd/throng." 

Aeneas throws the crowd into confusion, driving them with weapons through the leafy groves; *agens* and *miscet* work together to depict active pursuit and disruption of the enemy forces amid wooded terrain.

lines.original: nec prius absistit, quam septem ingentia victor
lines.english: nor does he cease before as victor he lays seven huge bodies on the ground and matches the number with his ships.
lines.gloss:
**nec prius absistit, quam septem ingentia victor**

*nec* (negative conjunction, "nor, and not"); *prius* (adverb, "before, sooner"); *absistit* (3rd sg. pres. indic. of *absisto*, "he ceases, withdraws"); *quam* (conjunction, "than, until"); *septem* (indeclinable numeral, "seven"); *ingentia* (neut. pl. acc. of *ingens*, "huge [bodies]"); *victor* (nom. sg., "victor, conqueror"). Aeneas does not cease his rampage until, as victor, he has slain seven huge warriors, matching the number of his ships (burned by the Latins).

lines.original: corpora fundat humi, et numerum cum navibus aequet.
lines.english: and lays seven massive bodies on the ground, matching the number with his ships.
lines.gloss:
**corpora fundat humi, et numerum cum navibus aequet.**

*corpora* (n. acc. pl., "bodies") – direct object of *fundat*; *fundat* (3rd sg. pres. subj., "he lays low/pours out") – jussive subjunctive completing the action of *absistit*; *humi* (locative, "on the ground"); *numerum* (m. acc. sg., "the number") – direct object of *aequet*; *aequet* (3rd sg. pres. subj., "he may equal/match") – purpose or result clause. Aeneas slays seven stags, matching the number to his ships so each crew receives one.

lines.original: Hinc portum petit, et socios partitur in omnes.
lines.english: From there he seeks the harbor and divides his companions among all the ships.
lines.gloss: **Hinc** (adverb) "from here/hence"; **portum** (accusative singular, m.) "harbor, port"; **petit** (3rd singular present active indicative, *peto*) "seeks, makes for"; **partitur** (3rd singular present deponent indicative, *partior*) "divides, distributes"; **socios** (accusative plural, m.) "companions, comrades" (object of distribution); **omnes** (accusative plural, m.) "all" (modifying an understood group). Aeneas departs from the site of the games and heads toward the harbor, distributing his companions/crews among all (the ships).

lines.original: Vina bonus quae deinde cadis onerarat Acestes
lines.english: Wine which good Acestes had then loaded in casks
lines.gloss: **Vina** (n. acc. pl., "wines") **bonus** (adj. nom. sg. m., "good/noble") **cadis** (n. abl. pl., "in jars") **onerarat** (v. plpf. 3rd sg., "had loaded") **Acestes** (n. nom. sg., "Acestes"). Aeneas distributes among all his comrades the wines which the good/noble hero Acestes had previously loaded into jars. The pluperfect indicates Acestes' prior hospitality on the Sicilian shore.

lines.original: litore Trinacrio dederatque abeuntibus heros,
lines.english: which the hero Acestes had given to them departing from the Trinacrian shore,
lines.gloss:
**litore Trinacrio dederatque abeuntibus heros**

*litore* (n. abl. sg.) "on the shore," ablative of place where; *Trinacrio* (adj. abl. sg.) "Trinacrian/Sicilian," modifying *litore*; *dederat* (pluperfect 3rd sg. of *do*) "had given"; *-que* (enclitic conj.) "and"; *abeuntibus* (pres. part. dat./abl. pl. of *abeo*) "to those departing"; *heros* (nom. sg.) "the hero" (Acestes). Acestes, the hero, had given these wines on the Sicilian shore to the Trojans as they were departing.

lines.original: dividit, et dictis maerentia pectora mulcet:
lines.english: He shares it out and soothes their sorrowing hearts with words.
lines.gloss:
**dividit, et dictis maerentia pectora mulcet:**

*dividit* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *divido*) "he divides/distributes"; *dictis* (abl. pl. neut. of *dictum*) "with words"; *maerentia* (acc. pl. neut. pres. act. part. of *maereo*) "grieving/sorrowing"; *pectora* (acc. pl. neut. of *pectus*) "hearts/breasts"; *mulcet* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *mulceo*) "he soothes/calms." Aeneas distributes provisions on the Sicilian shore and soothes his men's grieving hearts with words of encouragement.

lines.original: O socii—neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum—
lines.english: O comrades—for we are not ignorant of evils before—
lines.gloss:
**Target line: O socii—neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum—**

**socii** (nom. pl., *socius*, -ī, m.): "comrades, companions"; **ignari** (nom. pl. m., *ignarus*, -a, -um + gen.): "ignorant of, unacquainted with"; **sumus** (1st pl. pres. ind., *sum*): "we are"; **malorum** (gen. pl. n., *malum*, -ī): "of evils, misfortunes." 

Aeneas addresses his men as comrades who are not inexperienced in suffering, having endured previous hardships (*ante*).

lines.original: O passi graviora, dabit deus his quoque finem.
lines.english: O you who have endured worse things, god will grant an end to these troubles too.
lines.gloss:
**O passi graviora, dabit deus his quoque finem.**

*passi* (perfect participle of *patior*, nominative plural masculine): "having suffered"; *graviora* (comparative neuter plural accusative of *gravis*): "more severe things, worse things"; *dabit* (future active indicative, third singular of *do*): "will give"; *finem* (accusative singular of *finis*): "an end." Aeneas addresses his companions as those who have endured even worse hardships, promising that god will grant an end even to these present troubles.

lines.original: Vos et Scyllaeam rabiem penitusque sonantis
lines.english: You have approached the Scyllan fury and the depths-resounding rocks
lines.gloss:
**Gloss for "Vos et Scyllaeam rabiem penitusque sonantis":**

*Vos* (2nd pers. pron., nom. pl.) "you"; *Scyllaeam* (adj., acc. sg. fem.) "of Scylla"; *rabiem* (noun, acc. sg. fem.) "rage, fury"; *penitus* (adv.) "deeply, far within"; *sonantis* (pres. part., acc. pl. fem.) "resounding, roaring." Aeneas reminds his men they have experienced Scylla's rage and the deeply resounding (rocks/caves), continuing his catalog of perils already survived.

lines.original: accestis scopulos, vos et Cyclopea saxa
lines.english:
You have approached the Scyaean rocks and the deep-resounding crags, you have even experienced the Cyclopes' boulders.


---

Wait, let me reconsider the line division. Looking at the Latin more carefully:

You have approached the cliffs and the rocks of the Cyclops.
lines.gloss:
**accestis scopulos, vos et Cyclopea saxa**

*accestis* (2nd pl. perf. ind. act. of *accedo*) "you approached"; *scopulos* (m. acc. pl.) "rocks, cliffs"; *vos* (nom. pl.) "you" (emphatic); *Cyclopea* (adj. n. acc. pl.) "Cyclopean, of the Cyclops"; *saxa* (n. acc. pl.) "rocks, crags." Aeneas reminds his men they have already survived both Scylla's treacherous rocks and the crags where the Cyclopes dwell, urging them to take courage from past perils overcome.

lines.original: experti: revocate animos, maestumque timorem
lines.english: You who have experienced the rocks and Cyclops' crags, recall your courage and cast off sad fear.
lines.gloss:
**experti**: perfect participle of *experior*, nominative/vocative plural masculine, "having experienced"
**revocate**: imperative plural of *revoco*, "call back, restore"
**animos**: accusative plural of *animus*, "spirits, courage"
**maestum**: accusative singular masculine of *maestus*, modifying *timorem*, "sorrowful, gloomy"
**timorem**: accusative singular of *timor*, "fear"

Aeneas urges his men, having experienced these perils, to recall their courage and banish despondent fear.

lines.original: mittite: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit.
lines.english: Perhaps someday it will be pleasing to remember even these things.
lines.gloss: **mittite** (verb, 2nd plural present active imperative of *mitto*): "send away," "dismiss"; **forsan** (adverb): "perhaps"; **haec** (demonstrative pronoun, neuter plural accusative): "these things"; **meminisse** (verb, perfect active infinitive of *memini*): "to remember"; **iuvabit** (verb, 3rd singular future active indicative of *iuvo*): "it will help," "it will please." Aeneas urges his men to cast aside their fear, suggesting that perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even these present hardships.

lines.original: Per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum
lines.english: Through various misfortunes, through so many perils of our affairs
lines.gloss:
**Per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum**

*per* (prep. + acc.) "through"; *varios* (adj. acc. pl. m.) "various, diverse"; *casus* (noun acc. pl. m.) "misfortunes, calamities"; *tot* (indecl. adj.) "so many"; *discrimina* (noun acc. pl. n.) "perils, crises"; *rerum* (noun gen. pl. f.) "of affairs, of circumstances." Aeneas recounts the multiple disasters and critical dangers they have endured on their journey, with anaphora of *per* emphasizing the relentless succession of trials.

lines.original: tendimus in Latium; sedes ubi fata quietas
lines.english: We make our way to Latium, where the fates reveal a peaceful home.
lines.gloss: **tendimus** (1st pl. pres. ind. of *tendo*) "we make our way, we strive toward"; **in Latium** (prep. + acc.) "to Latium"; **sedes** (acc. pl. of *sedes*) "dwelling-places, a home"; **ubi** (rel. adv.) "where"; **fata** (nom. pl. of *fatum*) "the fates, destiny"; **quietas** (acc. pl. fem. adj. from *quietus*) "peaceful, at rest." Aeneas declares their destined journey to Latium, where the fates promise a peaceful settlement after their many trials.

lines.original: ostendunt; illic fas regna resurgere Troiae.
lines.english: They show us where it is right for the kingdom of Troy to rise again.
lines.gloss:
**ostendunt; illic fas regna resurgere Troiae.**

*ostendunt* (3rd pl. pres. act. ind. of *ostendō*) "show, reveal" – the fates are the subject; *illic* (adv.) "there" – in Latium; *fas* (indecl. neut. noun, nom./acc.) "divine law, what is right"; *regna* (neut. pl. acc. of *regnum*) "kingdoms, realm" – acc. subject of the infinitive; *resurgere* (pres. act. inf. of *resurgō*) "to rise again." The fates reveal that there, in Latium, it is divinely ordained for Troy's kingdom to rise again.

lines.original: Durate, et vosmet rebus servate secundis.
lines.english: Endure, and preserve yourselves for better times.
lines.gloss:
**Durate, et vosmet rebus servate secundis.**

*Durate* (pres. impv. act. 2nd pl. of *duro*, "endure, hold out"); *vosmet* (emphatic acc. of *vos*, "yourselves"); *rebus secundis* (abl. pl. of *res secunda*, "favorable circumstances, better times"); *servate* (pres. impv. act. 2nd pl. of *servo*, "preserve, keep safe"). Aeneas exhorts his men to endure their present hardships and preserve themselves for the prosperous times to come, employing the emphatic reflexive pronoun and a dative of purpose construction with the ablative of attendant circumstances.

lines.original: Talia voce refert, curisque ingentibus aeger
lines.english: Such things he speaks with his voice, and sick with overwhelming cares he feigns hope in his expression, suppressing deep grief in his heart.
lines.gloss:
**Talia voce refert, curisque ingentibus aeger**

*Talia* (neut. pl. acc., "such things") is the object of *refert* (3rd sg. pres., "he reports/speaks"). *Voce* (abl. sg., "with voice/in speech") indicates means. *Curisque ingentibus* (abl. pl., "and with/by huge cares") is ablative of cause modifying *aeger* (nom. sg. adj., "sick/troubled"). Aeneas speaks these encouraging words while inwardly suffering from overwhelming anxieties.

lines.original: spem voltu simulat, premit altum corde dolorem.
lines.english: He feigns hope in his expression, suppressing deep grief in his heart.
lines.gloss: **spem** (acc. sing., "hope") **voltu** (abl. sing., "in his face/expression") **simulat** (3rd sing. pres., "feigns/pretends"), **premit** (3rd sing. pres., "suppresses/hides") **altum** (acc. sing., "deep") **corde** (abl. sing., "in his heart") **dolorem** (acc. sing., "grief/pain"). Aeneas outwardly feigns hope in his expression but inwardly suppresses his deep grief in his heart, concealing his true anguish from his companions.

lines.original: Illi se praedae accingunt, dapibusque futuris;
lines.english: They gird themselves for the spoils and the feast to come.
lines.gloss:
**Gloss:**

*Illi* (nom. pl. masc., demonstrative pronoun) "those men"; *praedae* (dat. sg. fem., "praeda") "for the spoil/prey," dative of purpose; *accingunt* (3rd pl. pres. ind., "accingo") "gird themselves," "prepare"; *dapibusque* (dat. pl. fem., "daps") "-que" enclitic "and," "for the feast/banquet"; *futuris* (dat. pl. fem., future participle of "sum") "future," modifying "dapibus." Aeneas's men prepare themselves for their catch and the feast to come, girding themselves for butchering the game.

lines.original: tergora deripiunt costis et viscera nudant;
lines.english: They tear the hides from the ribs and lay bare the flesh.
lines.gloss:
**tergora deripiunt costis et viscera nudant**

*tergora* (n. acc. pl., "hides/skins"), *deripiunt* (3rd pl. pres. indic., "they tear off"), *costis* (f. abl. pl., "from the ribs"), *viscera* (n. acc. pl., "entrails/internal organs"), *nudant* (3rd pl. pres. indic., "they lay bare/expose"). The Trojans strip the hides from the deer's ribs and expose the internal organs, continuing their methodical butchering of the catch in preparation for the feast.

lines.original: pars in frusta secant veribusque trementia figunt;
lines.english: Some cut the flesh into pieces and fix the quivering parts on spits.
lines.gloss: **pars** (nom. f., "a part [of the men]"), **frusta** (acc. n. pl., "into pieces/chunks"), **secant** (3rd pl. pres., "they cut"), **veribusque** (abl. m. pl., "and on spits"), **trementia** (acc. n. pl., "trembling/quivering"), **figunt** (3rd pl. pres., "they fix/pierce"). Some men cut the meat into chunks and pierce the still-quivering pieces onto spits, continuing the butchering scene as they prepare to cook the slaughtered cattle.

lines.original: litore aena locant alii, flammasque ministrant.
lines.english: Others set bronze cauldrons on the shore and feed the flames.
lines.gloss:
**litore aena locant alii, flammasque ministrant.**

*litore* (abl. sg. n., "on the shore") – ablative of place where; *aena* (acc. pl. n., "bronze cauldrons/cooking pots") – direct object of *locant*; *locant* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic., "place, set up") – main verb; *alii* (nom. pl. m., "others") – subject; *flammas* (acc. pl. f., "flames, fires") – direct object of *ministrant*; *ministrant* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic., "supply, tend"). Others set up bronze cauldrons on the shore and tend the fires, as the Trojans prepare their meal after the storm.

lines.original: Tum victu revocant vires, fusique per herbam
lines.english: Then they restore their strength with food, and sprawled through the grass they feast on aged wine and rich venison.
lines.gloss:
**Tum** (adv.) "then"; **victu** (abl. sg. m. of *victus*) "by food/nourishment"; **revocant** (3rd pl. pres. act. indic. of *revoco*) "they restore/call back"; **vires** (acc. pl. f. of *vis*) "strength"; **fusi** (nom. pl. m. perf. pass. part. of *fundo*) "having been poured out/sprawled."

Then they restore their strength by food, and sprawled through the grass, they proceed to the actions described in the next line.

lines.original: implentur veteris Bacchi pinguisque ferinae.
lines.english: They fill themselves with aged wine and rich venison.
lines.gloss:
**implentur veteris Bacchi pinguisque ferinae.**

*implentur* (3rd pl. pres. pass. ind., *impleo*) "they are filled/sated"; *veteris* (gen. sg. m./n., *vetus*) "of aged/old," modifying *Bacchi*; *Bacchi* (gen. sg., *Bacchus*) "of Bacchus," i.e., wine (metonymy); *pinguis* (gen. sg. f., *pinguis*) "of rich/fat"; *ferinae* (gen. sg. f., *ferina*) "of game/venison." The Trojans fill themselves with aged wine and rich venison, the genitives depending on the passive verb of filling.

lines.original: Postquam exempta fames epulis mensaeque remotae,
lines.english: After hunger was banished by the feast and the tables were removed
lines.gloss: **Postquam** (conjunction) "after"; **exempta** (perfect passive participle, nominative feminine singular, from *eximō*) "removed, satisfied"; **fames** (nominative singular) "hunger"; **epulis** (ablative plural) "by the feast/banquet"; **mensae** (nominative plural) "tables"; **remotae** (perfect passive participle, nominative feminine plural, from *removeō*) "removed, cleared away." After their hunger was satisfied by the feast and the tables were cleared away, the Trojans turn to conversation about their lost companions.

lines.original: amissos longo socios sermone requirunt,
lines.english: They seek their lost companions in long conversation, uncertain between hope and fear whether to believe them living.
lines.gloss:
**Target line:** *amissos longo socios sermone requirunt*

**Key words:** 
- *amissos* (perfect passive participle, accusative masculine plural, from *amitto*): "lost"
- *socios* (accusative masculine plural, from *socius, -i*): "companions"
- *longo sermone* (ablative of means, from *longus, -a, -um* and *sermo, -onis*): "with long conversation/discourse"
- *requirunt* (3rd person plural present active indicative, from *requiro*): "they seek/ask about"

After the feast is removed, they ask about their lost companions with lengthy conversation, inquiring whether to believe them alive or dead.

lines.original: spemque metumque inter dubii, seu vivere credant,
lines.english: uncertain between hope and fear, whether to believe them living or suffering their last end and hearing their calls no more
lines.gloss:
**spemque metumque inter dubii, seu vivere credant,**

*spemque* (acc. fem. sg. of *spes*, "hope") and *metumque* (acc. masc. sg. of *metus*, "fear") frame *inter* (prep. + acc., "between"), describing the emotional state of the *dubii* (nom. masc. pl. of *dubius*, "uncertain" or "doubting"). *seu* (conj., "whether") introduces an indirect question with *credant* (3rd pl. pres. subj. of *credo*, "they believe") and *vivere* (pres. inf., "to live/be alive"). Aeneas's men waver between hope and fear, uncertain whether to believe their lost comrades still live.

lines.original: sive extrema pati nec iam exaudire vocatos.
lines.english: or whether they suffer their last end and no longer hear those calling them.
lines.gloss: **sive** (conj.) "or" – continuing the indirect question after *dubii*; **extrema** (n. pl. acc.) "final things, death" – object of *pati*; **pati** (pres. inf.) "to suffer, endure" – parallel to *vivere* in the previous line; **exaudire** (pres. inf.) "to hear" – second infinitive depending on the implied subject; **vocatos** (m. pl. acc., perf. pass. partic. of *voco*) "those being called" – i.e., themselves when summoned. The Trojans wonder whether their companions still live or have met death and can no longer hear their names being called out.

lines.original: Praecipue pius Aeneas nunc acris Oronti,
lines.english: Especially pious Aeneas now mourns the fate of fierce Orontes,
lines.gloss: **Praecipue** (adv., "especially") **pius** (adj., nom. sg. m., "dutiful/pious") **Aeneas** (nom. sg., "Aeneas") **acris** (adj., gen. sg. m., "fierce/spirited") **Oronti** (gen. sg., "of Orontes"). Aeneas, characterized by his defining epithet *pius*, grieves especially for the loss of fierce Orontes, whose name appears in the genitive of lamentation, anticipating the mourning for Amycus in the following line.

lines.original: nunc Amyci casum gemit et crudelia secum
lines.english: now he laments the fate of Amycus and broods with himself on the cruel doom of Lycus
lines.gloss:
**Gloss:**

*casum* (acc. sing., m., "fall/death") — the direct object of *gemit*. *Amyci* (gen. sing., m., "of Amycus") — possessive genitive modifying *casum*. *gemit* (3rd sing. pres. act. indic., "laments/mourns") — main verb. *crudelia* (acc. pl. neut., "cruel things/fates") — second object of *gemit*, coordinate with *casum*. *secum* (abl. sing., "with himself") — indicates internal reflection. Aeneas mourns the death of Amycus and reflects privately upon the cruel fates (of his companions lost in the storm).

lines.original: fata Lyci, fortemque Gyan, fortemque Cloanthum.
lines.english: the fates of Lycus, and brave Gyas, and brave Cloanthus.
lines.gloss:
**fata Lyci, fortemque Gyan, fortemque Cloanthum.**

Key words: *fata* (n. acc. pl., "fates, doom"), *Lyci* (m. gen. sg., "of Lycus"), *fortem* (adj. acc. sg., "brave, strong"), *Gyan* (m. acc. sg., Greek name "Gyas"), *Cloanthum* (m. acc. sg., Greek name "Cloanthus"). The subject (likely the person mentioned in the previous line) mourns the cruel fate of Lycus and recalls brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus, all victims or companions in some tragic context.

lines.original: Et iam finis erat, cum Iuppiter aethere summo
lines.english: And now it was ending, when Jupiter from highest heaven
lines.gloss:
**Et iam finis erat, cum Iuppiter aethere summo**

*finis* (nom. sg. m.) "end"; *erat* (imperf. ind. act. 3rd sg., *sum*) "was"; *cum* (conj.) "when"; *Iuppiter* (nom. sg.) "Jupiter"; *aethere summo* (abl. sg. m., *aethēr, summus*) "from highest heaven/sky." 

The temporal clause marks Jupiter's intervention from the heights of heaven just as the contest was concluding.

lines.original: despiciens mare velivolum terrasque iacentis
lines.english: Looking down upon the sail-winged sea and the lands lying outspread
lines.gloss: **despiciens** (pres. part., nom. sg. m.) "looking down upon" — **mare velivolum** (acc. sg. n.) "the sail-winged/sail-bearing sea" — **terrasque** (acc. pl. f.) "and the lands" — **iacentis** (pres. part., acc. pl. f.) "lying (below)." Jupiter, gazing from heaven's summit, surveys the sea covered with sails and the lands spread out beneath him.

lines.original: litoraque et latos populos, sic vertice caeli
lines.english: and shores and widespread peoples, thus on heaven's summit
lines.gloss:
**litoraque et latos populos, sic vertice caeli**

*litoraque* (neut. acc. pl., "and the shores"), *latos* (adj. acc. pl. masc., "widespread/extensive"), *populos* (masc. acc. pl., "peoples"), *vertice* (masc. abl. sg., "from the peak/summit"), *caeli* (masc. gen. sg., "of heaven"). Jupiter gazes down from heaven's peak upon the shores and far-flung peoples below, preparing to fix his eyes specifically on Libya's kingdoms.

lines.original: constitit, et Libyae defixit lumina regnis.
lines.english: He stood upon heaven's summit and fixed his gaze upon the Libyan realms.
lines.gloss: **constitit** (perfect, 3rd sg. of *consisto*) "stood still" or "took his stand"; **Libyae** (genitive sg.) "of Libya"; **defixit** (perfect, 3rd sg. of *defigo*) "fixed" or "cast down"; **lumina** (neut. acc. pl.) "eyes" or "lights"; **regnis** (abl. pl. of *regnum*) "on the kingdoms." Jupiter stopped and fixed his gaze upon the Libyan realms, marking a transition from cosmic overview to focused attention on the unfolding action in Carthage.

lines.original: Atque illum talis iactantem pectore curas
lines.english: And as he was turning over such cares in his heart
lines.gloss: **Gloss:** *Atque* (conj.): "and"; *illum* (acc. sing. masc. demonstrative): "him," referring to Aeneas; *talis* (acc. pl. fem. adj.): "such," modifying *curas*; *iactantem* (acc. sing. masc. pres. act. participle of *iacto*): "tossing, turning over"; *pectore* (abl. sing. neut.): "in his breast/heart," ablative of place where; *curas* (acc. pl. fem.): "cares, anxieties," direct object. The line depicts Aeneas mentally wrestling with such troubles in his heart when someone (Venus, in the next line) approaches him.

lines.original: tristior et lacrimis oculos suffusa nitentis
lines.english: Venus addressed him with eyes shining yet clouded with tears and sadder still
lines.gloss:
**Gloss on *tristior et lacrimis oculos suffusa nitentis*:**

*tristior* (comparative adjective, nominative singular feminine): "rather sad/sadder," modifying Venus; *lacrimis* (noun, ablative plural): "with tears," ablative of means; *oculos* (noun, accusative plural masculine): "eyes," direct object of *suffusa*; *suffusa* (perfect passive participle, nominative singular feminine): "having been filled/bedimmed," agreeing with the subject Venus; *nitentis* (present active participle, accusative plural masculine): "shining/bright," modifying *oculos*. Venus, appearing rather sad and with her bright eyes filled with tears, addresses Jupiter.

lines.original: O qui res hominumque deumque adloquitur Venus:
lines.english: O you who govern the affairs of men and gods, Venus addresses him,
lines.gloss:
**Target line: O qui res hominumque deumque**

**Key words:**
- *qui* (relative/interrogative pronoun, nom. masc. sing.) = "who" (referring to Jupiter)
- *res* (noun, acc. fem. pl.) = "affairs, matters"
- *hominumque* (noun, gen. masc. pl. + enclitic -que) = "and of men"
- *deumque* (noun, gen. masc. pl. + enclitic -que) = "and of gods"

Venus addresses Jupiter as "O you who [govern] the affairs of both men and gods," establishing his supreme authority before her supplication.

lines.original: aeternis regis imperiis, et fulmine terres,
lines.english: You who rule the affairs of men and gods with eternal commands and terrify with your thunderbolt
lines.gloss:
**aeternis regis imperiis, et fulmine terres**

*aeternis* (adj., abl. pl. neut.) "eternal" modifies *imperiis*; *regis* (2nd sg. pres. act. indic. of *rego*) "you rule"; *imperiis* (abl. pl. neut. of *imperium*) "commands, sway"; *fulmine* (abl. sg. neut. of *fulmen*) "thunderbolt"; *terres* (2nd sg. pres. act. indic. of *terreo*) "you terrify." Venus asks Jupiter why he governs with eternal commands and terrifies with his thunderbolt, setting up her complaint about Aeneas's suffering.

lines.original: quid meus Aeneas in te committere tantum,
lines.english: What wrong could my Aeneas commit against you so great,
lines.gloss:
**quid** (interrog. pron., neut. acc. sing.) = "what"; **Aeneas** (proper noun, nom. sing.) = "Aeneas"; **committere** (verb, perf. act. infin.) = "to commit, do wrong"; **tantum** (adv.) = "so great a thing, so much"; **in te** (prep. + acc.) = "against you." 

Venus asks Jupiter what great offense Aeneas could have committed against him to warrant such suffering, with *quid...tantum* framing the indirect question of what terrible crime deserves this punishment.

lines.original: quid Troes potuere, quibus, tot funera passis,
lines.english: what could the Trojans do, who having suffered so many deaths,
lines.gloss:
**Target line:** *quid Troes potuere, quibus, tot funera passis*

**Gloss:** *quid* (interrogative pronoun, accusative neuter singular) "what"; *Troes* (noun, nominative plural) "the Trojans"; *potuere* (perfect active indicative, 3rd plural of *possum*) "were able" or "could do"; *quibus* (relative pronoun, dative plural) "to whom"; *funera* (noun, accusative neuter plural) "deaths" or "disasters"; *passis* (perfect passive participle of *patior*, dative/ablative plural) "having suffered." The line asks what the Trojans could have done (to deserve their fate), they who have suffered so many calamities.

lines.original: cunctus ob Italiam terrarum clauditur orbis?
lines.english: Is the whole world of lands closed off to them because of Italy?
lines.gloss:
**cunctus ob Italiam terrarum clauditur orbis?**

*cunctus* (adj. nom. sg. m.) "entire, whole" modifies *orbis*; *ob* (prep. + acc.) "on account of, because of" governs *Italiam*; *terrarum* (gen. pl. f.) "of lands" partitive genitive with *orbis*; *clauditur* (3rd sg. pres. pass. indic.) "is shut, is closed"; *orbis* (nom. sg. m.) "world, circle." The line asks rhetorically whether the entire world of lands is closed to the Trojans on account of Italy alone.

lines.original: Certe hinc Romanos olim, volventibus annis,
lines.english: Surely from here the Romans one day, as the years roll by,
lines.gloss: **Certe** (adverb): "certainly, assuredly"; **hinc** (adverb): "from here/this source"; **Romanos** (accusative plural masculine of *Romanus*, -a, -um): "Romans" (object of implied verb); **olim** (adverb): "one day, at some future time"; **volventibus annis** (ablative absolute, present participle of *volvo*, -ere + ablative plural of *annus*, -i m.): "with the years rolling on, as time passes." Jupiter assures Venus that Romans will indeed arise from this Trojan lineage in the fullness of time.

lines.original: hinc fore ductores, revocato a sanguine Teucri,
lines.english: from here would come leaders, restored from the blood of Teucer
lines.gloss: **hinc** (adv.) "from here/hence"; **fore** (fut. inf. of *sum*) "would be"; **ductores** (nom. pl. m.) "leaders/commanders"; **revocato** (abl. sg. m., perf. pass. part. of *revoco*) "recalled/renewed"; **sanguine** (abl. sg. m.) "from the blood"; **Teucri** (gen. sg. m.) "of Teucer" (i.e., Troy). Jupiter prophesies that from this Trojan line there would arise leaders through the renewal of Teucer's bloodline, continuing Rome's destined greatness.

lines.original: qui mare, qui terras omni dicione tenerent,
lines.english: who would hold the sea and lands in complete dominion
lines.gloss: **mare** (n. acc. sg.) "sea"; **terras** (f. acc. pl.) "lands"; **omni dicione** (f. abl. sg.) "with every dominion/sovereignty"; **tenerent** (3rd pl. impf. subj. of *teneo*) "would hold/possess." The relative clause describes future leaders who would hold sea and land under universal rule, continuing Jupiter's prophecy about Rome's destined empire.

lines.original: pollicitus, quae te, genitor, sententia vertit?
lines.english: Having promised this, what changed your mind, father?
lines.gloss:
**pollicitus** (perf. part. masc. nom. sg. of *polliceor*) "having promised"; **genitor** (nom. sg.) "father"; **sententia** (nom. sg.) "opinion, resolve"; **vertit** (perf. indic. 3rd sg. of *verto*) "has changed, turned." 

The speaker reproaches his father, asking what resolve has changed him from what he had promised (regarding those who would hold sea and lands with universal sway).

lines.original: Hoc equidem occasum Troiae tristisque ruinas
lines.english: With this indeed I used to console myself for Troy's fall and sad destruction
lines.gloss:
**Hoc equidem occasum Troiae tristisque ruinas**

*Hoc* (demonstrative pronoun, accusative neuter singular) "this"; *equidem* (adverb) "indeed, truly"; *occasum* (noun, accusative masculine singular) "fall, destruction"; *Troiae* (proper noun, genitive singular) "of Troy"; *tristis* (adjective, accusative feminine plural) "sad, grievous"; *ruinas* (noun, accusative feminine plural) "ruins, collapse." Aeneas declares that this (promise or consolation) indeed balanced Troy's fall and grievous ruin against contrary fates, explaining what consoled him amid his losses.

lines.original: solabar, fatis contraria fata rependens;
lines.english: I took comfort in this, weighing fates set against fates.
lines.gloss: **solabar** (impf. indic. 1st sg. of *solor*) "I was consoling/comforting [myself]"; **fatis** (abl. pl. of *fatum*) "by/with fates"; **contraria** (nom./acc. neut. pl. of *contrarius*) "opposing, contrary"; **rependens** (pres. part. of *rependo*) "balancing, weighing in return." Dido explains she consoled herself for Troy's fall by reflecting that opposing fates balance each other out—her own disasters offset by the universal suffering she now witnesses.

lines.original: nunc eadem fortuna viros tot casibus actos
lines.english: Now the same fortune pursues men driven through so many disasters.
lines.gloss: **fortuna** (nom. sg. f.) "fortune" / "fate"; **viros** (acc. pl. m.) "men"; **tot** (indecl. adj.) "so many"; **casibus** (abl. pl. m.) "misfortunes" / "disasters"; **actos** (acc. pl. m., perf. pass. partic. of *ago*) "driven" / "harassed." Now the same fortune drives men harassed by so many disasters, continuing the theme of cruel fate's reversals.

lines.original: insequitur. Quem das finem, rex magne, laborum?
lines.english: pursues us. What end of our labors do you grant, great king?
lines.gloss:
**insequitur. Quem das finem, rex magne, laborum?**

*insequitur* (3rd sg. pres. indic. act. of *insequor*) "pursues, follows upon"; *quem* (acc. sg. masc. of interrog. *quis*) "what"; *finem* (acc. sg. masc. of *finis*) "end, limit"; *rex magne* (voc. sg. masc.) "great king" (addressing Jupiter); *laborum* (gen. pl. of *labor*) "of toils, labors." Juno asks Jupiter what end he grants to the Trojans' sufferings as their same fortune continues to pursue them.

lines.original: Antenor potuit, mediis elapsus Achivis,
lines.english: Antenor was able, having slipped through the midst of the Greeks,
lines.gloss: **Antenor** (nom. sg. m., proper noun) "Antenor" (Trojan elder who escaped Troy); **potuit** (3rd sg. perf. act. indic., *possum*) "was able"; **mediis** (abl. pl. m./n., *medius -a -um*) "from the midst of"; **elapsus** (nom. sg. m. perf. pass. part., *elabor*) "having escaped/slipped away"; **Achivis** (abl. pl. m., *Achivus -i*) "the Greeks/Achaeans." Venus laments that Antenor successfully escaped through the Greek forces and reached safety, implying contrast with Aeneas's continued wandering.

lines.original: Illyricos penetrare sinus, atque intima tutus
lines.english: to pierce the Illyrian gulfs and safely reach the inmost realms of the Liburnians
lines.gloss:
**Illyricos penetrare sinus, atque intima tutus**

*Illyricos* (acc. pl. m., "Illyrian") modifies *sinus* (acc. pl. m., "bays, gulfs"); *penetrare* (pres. act. inf., "to penetrate, reach") governs the accusatives and depends on *potuit* from the previous line; *intima* (acc. pl. n., "innermost regions") is the object of an understood verb of motion; *tutus* (nom. sg. m., "safe, unharmed") agrees with Antenor as subject. Antenor safely penetrated the Illyrian gulfs and reached the innermost territories.

lines.original: regna Liburnorum, et fontem superare Timavi,
lines.english: and the realms of the Liburni, and pass beyond the source of Timavus
lines.gloss:
**regna Liburnorum, et fontem superare Timavi**

*regna* (n. acc. pl., "kingdoms/realms") Liburnorum (gen. pl., "of the Liburnians," an Illyrian people); *fontem* (m. acc. sg., "source/spring") Timavi (gen. sg., "of the Timavus," a river in northeastern Italy); *superare* (inf., "to pass over/surmount"). Antenor's journey continues past the territories of the Liburnians and beyond the source of the Timavus river.

lines.original: unde per ora novem vasto cum murmure montis
lines.english: whence through nine mouths with vast roar from the mountain it bursts forth as a sea and overwhelms the fields with resounding flood
lines.gloss:
**Target line:** *unde per ora novem vasto cum murmure montis*

**Key words:** *unde* (adv., "from where/whence"), *ora* (n. pl. acc., "mouths/openings"), *novem* (indecl. adj., "nine"), *murmure* (n. abl. sg., "roaring/rumbling"), *montis* (n. gen. sg., "of the mountain").

The Timavus river bursts forth through nine mouths with the vast roaring of the mountain, a geological phenomenon in northeastern Italy where the river emerges from underground channels.

lines.original: it mare proruptum et pelago premit arva sonanti.
lines.english: The sea bursts forth and overwhelms the fields with its resounding flood.
lines.gloss:
**it mare proruptum et pelago premit arva sonanti.**

*it* (verb, 3rd sg. pres. indic. of *eo*) "goes, rushes"; *proruptum* (perf. pass. partic. neut. nom. sg. of *prorumpo*) "having burst forth"; *pelago* (noun, abl. sg.) "with sea/flood"; *premit* (verb, 3rd sg. pres. indic. of *premo*) "presses down, overwhelms"; *arva* (noun, neut. acc. pl.) "fields"; *sonanti* (pres. partic. abl. sg. of *sono*) "resounding, roaring." The sea, having burst forth, rushes onward and overwhelms the fields with its roaring flood.

lines.original: Hic tamen ille urbem Patavi sedesque locavit
lines.english: Yet here he founded the city of Patavium and established a settlement for the Trojans.
lines.gloss:
**Hic tamen ille urbem Patavi sedesque locavit**

*Hic* (adverb) "here"; *tamen* (conjunction) "nevertheless, yet"; *ille* (demonstrative pronoun, nom. sg.) "that man, he" (referring to Antenor); *urbem* (noun, acc. sg. fem.) "city" (direct object); *Patavi* (proper noun, gen. sg.) "of Patavium" (modern Padua); *sedesque* (noun, acc. pl. fem., with enclitic *-que*) "and settlements"; *locavit* (verb, perfect active indicative, 3rd sg.) "placed, established." Antenor, though entering Italy under these circumstances, founded the city of Patavium and established settlements for his people.

lines.original: Teucrorum, et genti nomen dedit, armaque fixit
lines.english: He gave a name to the Trojan people, established their arms, and fixed them there.
lines.gloss: **Teucrorum** (genitive plural of *Teucrī*) "of the Trojans"; **genti** (dative singular of *gēns*) "to the people"; **nomen** (accusative singular, neuter noun) "a name"; **dedit** (perfect, 3rd singular of *dō*) "he gave"; **armaque** (accusative plural of *arma*, with enclitic *-que*) "and arms"; **fixit** (perfect, 3rd singular of *fīgō*) "he fixed/hung up." Antenor gave a name to the Trojan people and dedicated/hung up his arms, completing the foundation of Patavium.

lines.original: Troia; nunc placida compostus pace quiescit:
lines.english: Troy; now settled in tranquil peace he rests:
lines.gloss: **Troia;** (ablative of place) "at/in Troy"; **placida ... pace** (ablative of manner) "in peaceful peace/calm peace"; **compostus** (perfect passive participle, nominative singular masculine) "laid to rest, settled"; **quiescit** (present indicative, 3rd singular) "he rests." Dardanus, having founded Troy and given his name to the Trojans, now rests peacefully in death, laid to rest in tranquil repose.

lines.original: nos, tua progenies, caeli quibus adnuis arcem,
lines.english: We, your offspring, to whom you promise the heights of heaven,
lines.gloss: **nos** (pronoun, acc. pl., "us"), **progenies** (noun, nom. sg., "offspring/descendants"), **caeli** (noun, gen. sg., "of heaven"), **adnuis** (verb, 2nd sg. pres., "you grant/promise"), **arcem** (noun, acc. sg., "citadel/heights"). Venus continues her complaint to Jupiter: "we, your offspring, to whom you promise the citadel of heaven," emphasizing the broken promise to her Trojan descendants who should inherit divine favor and rule.

lines.original: navibus (infandum!) amissis, unius ob iram
lines.english: we who have lost our ships—unspeakable!—because of one goddess's wrath
lines.gloss:
**navibus (infandum!) amissis, unius ob iram**

*navibus* (f. pl. abl.): "our ships," ablative absolute with *amissis*. *infandum* (n. acc. sg., gerundive of *for*): "unspeakable thing," exclamatory accusative. *amissis* (perf. pass. part., abl. pl.): "having been lost," completing the ablative absolute construction. *unius* (gen. sg.): "of one (goddess)," referring to Juno. *ob iram* (f. acc. sg.): "on account of (her) wrath," explaining the cause of their loss.

lines.original: prodimur atque Italis longe disiungimur oris.
lines.english: We are betrayed and kept far apart from the Italian shores.
lines.gloss:
**prodimur atque Italis longe disiungimur oris.**

*prodimur* (1st pl. pres. pass. indic. of *prodo*, "we are betrayed/abandoned"); *atque* (conj., "and"); *Italis* (abl. pl. adj. modifying *oris*, "from Italian"); *disiungimur* (1st pl. pres. pass. indic. of *disjungo*, "we are separated"); *oris* (abl. pl. of *ora*, "from shores/coasts").
